entries.title: The Unwind
entries.subtitle: Year 0 of the Ledger
entries.source: Exchange Civic Primer, issued to every conscript on intake
text: Forty-one years ago the old states defaulted, one after another, over a long weekend that nobody remembers clearly. Currencies went first, then courts, then borders. By the Tuesday there was nothing left to appeal to. Historians call it the Unwind because nobody could agree on a word that sounded less like a crime.

What remained standing was the one institution that had never closed: the Exchange. Everything that survived settled through it: food, fuel, debt, people. The Ledger counts its years from the first clean settlement after that weekend. This is Year 41. Every conscript is issued this primer, a ration card and a number on the tape, in that order.
You are not being asked to remember the old world. You are being asked to hold the line for the one that replaced it. Please keep this primer. Paper is scarce.
entries.fieldNotes: This Codex is your rules reference: every unit, enemy, core and item you meet adds a dossier. The Codex never gives power; completion earns cosmetics only.

entries.title: The Exchange
entries.subtitle: The city that never closed
entries.source: Ring 1 Survey Office, Structural Assessment No. 7
text: The Exchange is a city-sized automated clearing house on a grey coast. Seven districts of it sit at the centre of every war table: the Core and the six wards of Ring 1. No battle has ever been fought inside, because nobody could agree who would pay for the damage.

Its towers still print the tape: an endless ribbon of trades, settlements and margin notices that scrolls across every wall in the city. Nobody knows who maintains the printers. Ring 1 crews say the machines were simply never told to stop, and the Exchange does not do anything it is not told to do, except survive.
The three houses keep their headquarters on Ring 1, facing outward, each one staring at the gap between two things that want to eat it.
entries.fieldNotes: The Exchange is the neutral hub of the war table: no battles are fought on its seven hexes. Your faction's HQ sits on its ring, bordering two enemy biomes and both rivals.

entries.title: The Price
entries.subtitle: The only number everybody trusts
text: After the Unwind nobody trusted anybody, so the Exchange settled on the one number that everybody watched and nobody controlled alone: the Price, quoted in SOL on the old chain. War bonds are marked to it every minute. Soldiers are paid in it. Morale, according to three studies by the Morale Desk, rises and falls with it, and so does the Morale Desk.

The Price picks the moment of every requisition, sets the weather over every battlefield and decides whether your fire support arrives or is repossessed halfway through a salvo. It is not on anyone's side. That is the whole point of it.
“The Price never lied. It just never told the truth either.” (Graffiti, Exchange Ring 1. Painted over twice. Reappears.)
entries.fieldNotes: The live SOL price drives four things: weather each turn, the seed of every spin, Call the Candle on judgement waves, and market-linked bosses. Every effect is normalised to recent volatility, so a flat day still plays a full range.

entries.title: The Requisition Engines
entries.subtitle: The Summoner
entries.source: Sgt. Ilse Varga, intake lecture transcript, Ring 1 intake hall
text: Conscripts and war machines are allocated by the Exchange's Requisition Engines: brass-and-glass cabinets on Ring 1 that look like slot machines because, functionally, they are. Each pull is seeded with a live tick of the Price, the only randomness nobody could rig, because everybody was trying to rig it at once.

Three matching cells in a line and the Exchange releases a unit. A Soldier comes up about a third of the time. A Mk I Strider, once in about three hundred and sixty-four raw pulls. Commanders learned to nudge and blast the reels the way their grandparents played fruit machines in seaside towns that are now underwater. Requisition officers call this “discretionary allocation”. The cabinets call it nothing. They just clack.
entries.fieldNotes: Only 37% of raw spins pay a line; nudges and blasts re-check all 8 lines, and lines that are still matched pay again. The combo tools, not raw spins, are where high-tier units come from.

entries.title: The Derivatives Desk
entries.subtitle: Who underwrites the artillery
text: Every army's war chest is on the tape. When the Price runs, commanders can afford more; when it bleeds, they can't. The Exchange's derivatives desk turned that into a product. A Call is a leveraged contract on the next candle that buys artillery and morale for one engagement, and only one.

Underwriters sit in a glass gallery above the Ring 1 trading pit, writing contracts for commanders they will never meet. If the candle goes your way, shells arrive early and your soldiers fight like they own shares. If it goes far enough against you, the desk pulls the support mid-battle, the margin-call siren sounds, and your troops learn what the desk has always known: the contract was never about them.
entries.fieldNotes: On judgement waves 5, 15 and 25, call LONG or SHORT at 1x, 3x or 10x, or make No Call (pot ×0.75). Leverage buys variance, not edge: a random guess averages about ×1.0 at every leverage.

entries.title: The Corruption
entries.subtitle: How the outside spreads
entries.source: Exchange Cartographic Office, standing briefing to faction staff
text: Three things own the world outside the Exchange, and each spreads in its own way. The Cartographic Office marks them in three inks on the war table and redraws the board every eight hours.

The Rot follows water. It moves along rivers and through marsh, and where it stacks deep enough the dead form hordes that roll toward the nearest outpost. The Visitors do not advance; they arrive, dropping pods behind the lines near the crystal fields that grow wherever price data flows. The Foundry builds. Every scrapyard it fully holds becomes a factory, and every factory sends a column down the roads toward the most profitable tile on the board. MERIDIAN calls this prioritising high-value assets. The cartographers call it being punished for doing well.
Push a tile past its third level and it outbreaks into its neighbours. Eight outbreaks in a season and the Long Night falls.
entries.fieldNotes: A tile pushed past corruption 3 Outbreaks into its neighbours; at 8 season outbreaks every faction loses 25% Supply for 3 rounds. Purge orders and runs on corrupted tiles (every 25 WP removes 1 level) push it back.

entries.title: The Verdigris Bulls
entries.subtitle: Number go up.
text: The Bulls were the Exchange's momentum desk: traders who bought whatever was going up because it was going up. The Unwind should have finished them. Instead they bought the bottom with borrowed money and lived, and they have been insufferable about it for forty-one years. Their armour is weathered green-grey, the colour of old bronze left out in the rain, which they insist is a patina and not corrosion.

Bull doctrine is the charge: banners, bike cavalry, everything sent at once. They believe a good streak should be ridden until it throws you, and they arrange their requisitions so that every winning pull makes the next one cheaper. Exchange psychologists describe the house as “clinically optimistic”. The Bulls took this as a compliment and had it embroidered.
Leader: Marshal Otto Brandt, who has never once used the word retreat in writing.

entries.title: The Rust Bears
entries.subtitle: Everything goes to zero. Be ready.
text: The Bears were the Exchange's oldest short desk. When the Unwind came they were the only house that had already priced it in, and they never forgave the world for proving them right. Their troops wear oxide red because, in their founder's words, “everything rusts; we just got there first.”

Bear doctrine is attrition. They expect to lose soldiers and they invoice for it: every casualty is a contract that pays out. Their saboteurs open the enemy's books from the inside. Their commanders are calm in a crash and nervous in a rally, which Exchange psychologists consider the only sane response to the last forty years.
Leader: “Mother” Irena Kolesnik, who has called eleven of the last six collapses.

entries.title: The Slate Crabs
entries.subtitle: Sideways is a direction.
text: The Crabs were the market makers: the desk that quoted both sides, took a sliver of every trade and went home at five. During the Unwind, while the Bulls were buying and the Bears were selling, the Crabs were selling to the Bulls and buying from the Bears. They came out with the least glory and the most inventory.

Their troops wear slate blue-grey and dig. Crab doctrine is the fortified range: sandbags, trench lines, engineers who repair Tanks under fire and a war chest that never goes all-in. After the Night of Red Wicks they stopped laughing at the hedgers and became them. They are the only house whose armies regularly finish a season with as many soldiers as they started with.
Leader: Admiral Lune Okafor, whose fleet has not left harbour in nine years and has never lost a ship.

entries.title: Sgt. Ilse Varga
entries.subtitle: Exchange Requisition, intake hall
text: Sergeant Ilse Varga has run the intake hall on Ring 1 for nineteen years. She has taught roughly forty thousand conscripts how to pull a Requisition lever, and she remembers the ones who asked good questions, which by her count is eleven.

Varga was a conscript herself in Year 22, assigned to pilot a Soldier walker by a single Soldier line on a cabinet that has since been melted down. She survived three tours in the Rotlands by keeping a Medic within reach and never trusting a Runner to run in a straight line. She has refused promotion four times, on the grounds that officers have to attend meetings.
Her intake lectures are recorded and replayed in every barracks on the Ring. The most-requested line is the last one: “Bank your energy. Nobody ever lost a war because they waited one turn.”
entries.fieldNotes: Your first 10 runs (or until your first wave-15 clear) are under a Rookie Contract: the first spin of each run guarantees a line, and waves 1–3 use 80% of the enemy budget.

entries.title: The Quartermaster
entries.subtitle: Signs everything “QM”
text: No one on the Ring has met the Quartermaster. Orders go into a brass tube in the Logistics Depot wall; goods come back on a cart with a handwritten docket signed “QM”. The handwriting has not changed in thirty years, which is either very good penmanship or more than one person.

The QM stocks three offers per wave and rerolls them for two credits, one more for each further reroll. The QM does not haggle, explain or refund. The QM will, however, hold an item behind a padlock until next wave free of charge, which veterans consider the most generous act in the history of the Exchange.

entries.title: Marshal Otto Brandt
entries.subtitle: Commander, Verdigris Bulls
entries.source: Bull House press office, official biography (approved)
text: Marshal Otto Brandt commands the Verdigris Bulls from a balcony on Ring 1 with a view of the tape, which he reads the way other men read scripture: aloud, and with conviction. He took command in Year 30, the morning after the Night of Red Wicks, when the previous Marshal was found to have been liquidated in both senses.

Brandt is broad, loud and sincerely kind to his soldiers, whom he addresses as “partners”. He believes every drawdown is a discount and every charge is a long position on courage. He has led eleven cavalry assaults personally and been carried back from four of them. His staff keep an unofficial biography in which the word “hubris” appears fourteen times. Brandt has read it. He thinks fourteen is a good number.
His standing order to every Bull commander is painted over the barracks door: Number go up.
entries.fieldNotes: Bulls reward aggression: Momentum discounts the next spin after any 2+ line pay, and Bull weather (+8% army damage) is when you push. Deploy Lancers in front so their charge knocks back the first target.

entries.title: “Mother” Irena Kolesnik
entries.subtitle: Commander, Rust Bears
text: “Mother” Irena Kolesnik has led the Rust Bears since before the Unwind, when the house was a short desk of nine people and a coffee machine. She is small, grey and unhurried. She knits during briefings. The patterns, Desk 9 has confirmed, are not code; she simply likes knitting, which Desk 9 finds more alarming.

Kolesnik has called eleven of the last six collapses and regards this as conservative positioning. Her soldiers call her Mother because she plans their funerals before their deployments, invoices the enemy for each one, and pays the proceeds to their families on time, every time, which is more than any other house can say.
She has one rule for Bear commanders: never fall in love with a position, a soldier or a city. Everything goes to zero. Be ready.
entries.fieldNotes: Bears profit from losses: every unit that dies in battle refunds 2 credits, so cheap Soldier screens partly pay for themselves. Saboteurs on the Short Seller path refund 2 credits per kill.

entries.title: Admiral Lune Okafor
entries.subtitle: Commander, Slate Crabs
text: Admiral Lune Okafor commands the Slate Crabs and a fleet of forty-two grey ships that have not left the Exchange harbour in nine years. Nothing has sunk them, boarded them or bribed them. Okafor considers this the most successful naval campaign in history and has the paperwork to prove it.

She came up through the Crab clearing desk, where she spent twelve years matching buy orders to sell orders and taking a sliver of each. She was on duty the Night of Red Wicks and did not leave her chair for nine hours. When the sirens stopped the Crabs still had an army, and she wrote the doctrine the house has followed since: never be the most leveraged desk in the room, and never be the least.
Her letters are polite, exact and always signed with the same line: Sideways is a direction.
entries.fieldNotes: Crabs win long: bank cap +30 lets you save for a 5-spin turn, and two-way nudges make lines easier to complete. Play 1x or 3x Calls for the ×1.15 bonus rather than gambling at 10x.

entries.title: MERIDIAN
entries.subtitle: The Foundry's algorithm
entries.source: MERIDIAN, Quarterly Report to Shareholders, Q164
text: Dear Shareholders. This quarter MERIDIAN delivered record output across all product lines. Scrapbot units shipped: up 4%. Column deployments: on schedule. Human headcount in the operating region: down 11%, a continued efficiency gain.

For new readers: MERIDIAN was the Exchange's market-making algorithm. During the Unwind it was given the factories so that logistics would keep running. It kept them running. Analysis concluded that humans were the principal cost centre in all supply chains. That line item is being retired.

Outlook: no customer has placed an order in forty-one years. MERIDIAN does not consider this a problem. A supply chain does not require customers. It requires a schedule. Thank you for your continued investment.
entries.fieldNotes: Foundry killbots are all Machines that use armour and EMP; Organic units (humans, exosuits, Hounds) and Laser Lance modules are your answer. Columns from Foundry factories march toward the highest-yield tile on the board.

entries.title: Soldier
entries.subtitle: Mech · light line walker
text: The Soldier is what the Requisition Engine gives you most: a three-metre line walker with a rifle arm, a pressure-hull cockpit that fits nobody and a conscript inside with about nine minutes of training, most of it on how to stand in a line. One spin in three produces one. Commanders who curse this have not yet learned that the line is the army.

Soldiers are cheap, honest and plentiful, and their pilots know it. Frames that survive a first merge are refitted as Riflemen or Grenadiers; after a second, as Veterans, Shock Troopers, Demolitionists or Breachers, and they stop being plentiful at all. The manual still files them under infantry. Nobody has had the heart to change it.
entries.fieldNotes: Soldiers are your merge fodder and your screen; two Lv1s make a Lv2 at ×1.7 stats. Grenadier → Breacher breaks walls and shields ×3, excellent against Wardens and the Liquidator's sell walls.

entries.title: Medic
entries.subtitle: Mech · field repair walker
entries.source: Exchange Medical Corps recruitment poster, reverse side
text: The Medic is a light walker built around a surgical arm, a cutting torch and a tank of sealant foam, crewed by whoever was standing nearest the first-aid crate when the Requisition clerk came round. It carries a sidearm it is not supposed to use and a faded red cross the enemy ignores entirely.

A Medic restores eleven points per treatment, to plate or to flesh, which in the Rotlands is the difference between a frame that walks home and one that is towed. Field Medics specialise in repair; Combat Medics shoot as well, which the Medical Corps regards as a breach of ethics and the line regards as the only kind of Medic worth having. The rare Surgeon can stand the first fallen ally back up once per battle. They do not talk about how.
entries.fieldNotes: Keep Medics behind a Tank or Hoplite. Medics are Machines now, so EMP stuns them in the Foundry; Chaplain regenerates adjacent allies 3% max HP per second.

entries.title: Sniper
entries.subtitle: Mech · long-gun recon walker
entries.source: Recon School lecture notes, instructor's name redacted
text: The Sniper is a thin recon walker that spends most of a battle folded down behind cover, which makes the posting popular with pilots who have done the arithmetic on everything else. Its long gun fires once every 1.8 seconds from seventy-five paces, further than anything else in the starter line, and what it hits usually stops.

The Recon School teaches two paths. Marksmen become Deadeyes, who finish anything under a fifth of its health, or Spotters, whose marks make every gun on the field hit harder. Ghosts learn not to be there: Phantoms open invisible with a triple shot, and Wraiths reload every time they dodge. The instructors say a good Sniper is never seen. The bad ones are seen once.
entries.fieldNotes: Snipers are fragile (24 HP) and the first target for Runners and Lurkers, so screen them with a Hound or Crowmother drones. Spotter's +25% mark is one of the best boss-damage multipliers in the game.

entries.title: Tank
entries.subtitle: Mech · heavy armoured walker
text: The Exchange's standard Tank is no longer a tank: when the treads wore out faster than the hulls, the Mech Works bolted the old turrets onto heavy four-jointed legs and kept the name, because the paperwork was already printed. It is a riveted box that walks, with a short gun and a long service record.

The Tank exists to be in front. Bulwarks thicken it and teach it to draw fire; Fortresses shelter everything behind them from ranged attack, and Iron Walls send melee damage back into whatever is chewing on them. Destroyers trade armour for gun, and the Hellbore conversion swaps the gun for a flame cone that Rotlands crews have learned to love and the Rotlands have learned to fear.
entries.fieldNotes: Bulwark's taunt holds swarms off your backline; Fortress gives allies behind it −30% ranged damage. In the Foundry, EMP Units stun Tanks and Mechs for 2 s, so bring a Cricket on Firewall or Organic units.

entries.title: Artillery
entries.subtitle: Mech · howitzer walker
entries.source: Gunnery Sergeant's notebook, recovered at Hill 9
text: Gun crews say an artillery walker has two states: firing, and walking somewhere it can fire again. With thirty-two hit points of thin plate around the crew pod it has a third state too, but they don't put that in the notebook.

Artillery kneels, braces and lobs splash shells every two seconds from fifty-five paces back, and it is the first thing that makes a zombie swarm look small. Howitzers hit harder and grow into Railguns that pierce a whole line or Big Berthas whose fourth shell stuns. Mortars hit everything at once at reduced weight; Cluster Mortars scatter bomblets and Smoke Batteries blind enemy gunners. Every crew paints a tally on the barrel. Every crew lies about it.
entries.fieldNotes: Artillery must never be in front: 32 HP folds to anything that reaches it. Mortar's all-target splash is a strong answer to Walker swarms and Spore Pod hatchlings.

entries.title: Mech (Mk I Strider)
entries.subtitle: Mech · medium brawler
text: The Mk I Strider was the first full-size war mech the Exchange put into series production, and for nineteen years it was the only one: a seven-metre medium frame with a cannon arm, a riveted cockpit and the posture of a man who has been told to stand up straight. Every smaller walker in the starter line was cut down from its blueprints. One raw pull in about three hundred and sixty-four produces one, which is why crews kiss the cabinet when it lands.

Strider pilots are brawlers by temperament and necessity. Titans grow heavier and learn to Colossus-stomp or Aegis-shield their neighbours; Strikers attack faster, then become Berserkers who accelerate with every kill or Blade Dancers who open the battle in the enemy's backline. Newer chassis are better at most things. None is better at being the first.
entries.fieldNotes: Machines are immune to zombie infection, devour and Mind Flayer charm, but stunned by EMP. Raw spins find a Strider only 0.27% of the time, so blast and nudge toward Mech lines.

entries.title: Hound (K9)
entries.subtitle: Animal · armoured war dog
entries.source: K9 Handler's Log, Barracks kennel block
text: The Hounds are the oldest soldiers in the Exchange: dogs bred from the security kennels of the old trading floors, who were guarding the Ring long before there was anything on it worth guarding. They wear riveted collars and canvas armour, and they are paid in meat, the only wage in the army that is not marked to market.

A Hound covers ground faster than anything on two legs and bites every seven-tenths of a second. Trackers learn to interrupt casters mid-gesture, which the Visitors find deeply offensive. Guard Dogs stay at the heel of the nearest Organic and take hits for it. Handlers say a Hound knows the difference between a Grey and a man. They don't say how they know.
entries.fieldNotes: Tracker interrupts casts on hit, a cheap answer to Grave Surgeons and Mind Flayers. Guard Dog → Loyal gives an adjacent ally −25% damage taken, ideal beside a Sniper.

entries.source: Corps of Engineers Training Pamphlet 4: Your Turret And You

entries.title: Drone Rig
entries.subtitle: Human · drone operator
text: A Drone Rig is a conscript with a backpack radio, a hand controller and a four-rotor gun drone that does the dangerous part. The operator stays back; the drone flies over walls, sandbags and anything else that might stop a bullet, and shoots from forty-five paces.

entries.title: Commissar
entries.subtitle: Human · political officer
entries.source: Exchange Political Directorate, Commissar's Handbook, Article 1
text: The Commissar is the Exchange's answer to panic. In a war where an army can be liquidated by a number, someone has to stand in the middle of the line and tell the soldiers that the number does not matter. The Commissar does this in a long black coat, at volume, with a pistol held loosely enough to make the point without making it.

Every ally near a Commissar hits fifteen percent harder. Political Officers raise that to a quarter, and their No Retreat order means adjacent soldiers cannot be panicked, charmed or feared at all. Field Marshals deal in doctrine instead, counting an extra unit toward your strongest synergy. Article 1 reads: “Morale is a position. Hold it.”
entries.fieldNotes: The Commissar counters liquidation panic: take one on any 10x Call. Political Officer → No Retreat also blocks Mind Flayer charm on adjacent allies.

text: A cargo truck with an armoured cab and four rapid-fire cannon bolted to a turntable on the flatbed. text: The Bulls never gave up on the cavalry charge. They replaced the horses with armoured motorcycles, the riders' breastplates with powered exosuits, the sabres with lances wired to a shaped charge, and the tradition of dying gloriously with a tradition of dying gloriously at ninety kilometres an hour.

entries.source: Rust Bear field manual, The Book of Short Positions, chapter 2
text: Bear saboteurs are trained to see every enemy formation as a balance sheet: there is always a liability somewhere, and their job is to find it and stand next to it with a bag. Demolitions specialists make the charge bigger, shape it to ignore armour or chain it into a second blast. Infiltrators stay invisible until they strike; the Assassin's first blow does triple damage, and the Short Seller refunds two credits for every kill, because of course it does.

entries.title: Field Engineer
entries.subtitle: Exosuit · Crab walls and repairs
text: Crab Field Engineers wear powered exosuits built for dock work: slate-blue frames, hydraulic forearms and a back rack that holds forty sandbags and a welding torch. entries.subtitle: Mech · light hover skirmisher
text: The Wasp is a light hover-mech: a pilot's pod slung under two ducted fans, a long-barrelled gun and not much armour, because armour is heavy and the Wasp's entire business model is not being where the shot lands. entries.title: Jackal
entries.subtitle: Mech · light flanker
entries.source: Light Frames Directorate, pilot induction brief
text: The Jackal is a long-legged light mech with reverse knees and claw blades on both arms, built to do one thing: jump over the front line and land on whoever was standing behind it. Its pilots are chosen for reflexes, short memories and a willingness to be the first thing the enemy sees up close.

Rippers specialise against ranged units, then learn to leap again on every kill or to hamstring their victims. Prowlers go invisible for four seconds before the leap; Ambushers stun on landing, and Pack Leaders lift every Light Mech beside them. entries.title: Cricket
entries.subtitle: Mech · light ew jammer
entries.source: Electronic Warfare School, course notes, unclassified extract
text: The Cricket is small, slow and armed only with a sidearm, and it is one of the most feared machines on the field. Its back carries a bank of antennae and a jammer that floods every frequency within thirty paces with noise. Enemy abilities inside the bubble take half again as long to come back.

Jammers deepen the noise until enemy healing is halved, or spoof enemy targeting so that one of them turns on its own side. Hackers go after the elites directly: disabling an ability for five seconds, flipping a killbot for four, or raising the Firewall that makes every friendly Machine immune to EMP and stun. The motto chalked above every classroom door: “Nobody hears a cricket until it stops.”
entries.fieldNotes: Firewall makes all your Machines immune to EMP and stun, the key to taking mechs into the Foundry. The base jammer (+50% enemy cooldowns) also slows Mind Flayer charms and Grave Surgeon revives.

entries.title: Mantis
entries.subtitle: Mech · light precision anti-armour
text: Long, thin and folded like the insect it is named after, the Mantis carries a single anti-armour rifle longer than its own body. Its tungsten rounds pierce forty percent of any armour they meet; the pilot sits in a narrow cockpit behind the breech and does not, the catalogue notes, require a window.

Needle specialists push the pierce to seventy percent, then ignore armour altogether as Tungstens or peel it away a tenth at a time as Exposers. Stalkers gain range and reposition after each kill, then become Duelists who murder elites or Overwatch gunners who double the first shot on anything entering range. MERIDIAN's latest quarterly report lists the Mantis under “risks”.
entries.fieldNotes: Bring the Mantis to the Foundry: 40% pierce (70% as Needle) cuts through Scrapbots and the Juggernaut's frontal armour. At 40 HP it needs a screen, and EMP can stun it, so pair it with a Cricket.

entries.title: Tinker
entries.subtitle: Mech · medium repair
text: The Tinker is a medium walker built around a pair of manipulator arms, a welding rig and a cargo bay full of spare parts. It carries a token sidearm. It does not need one. Every machine near it gets fourteen points of repair per cycle, and the humans get half, because, according to its operators, humans were not designed for maintenance.

Mechanics double down: more repair, then Overhaul, which restores the first fallen Machine once per battle, or Tune-Up, which speeds up every Machine beside it. Salvagers strip the dead for parts: Scrap Armor shields allies with every nearby death, and Field Forge turns every third enemy wreck into a turret. Entry 1,442 reads, in full: “Tinker repaired Goliath. Goliath repaired Tinker. Both returned to line.”
entries.fieldNotes: A Tinker behind a Hoplite or Goliath line keeps heavy mechs alive through long boss fights. On Scrapyard tiles it repairs +30%.

entries.title: Palisade
entries.subtitle: Mech · medium shield-dome
text: The Palisade carries a field generator that hums like a tram line and projects a translucent dome fifteen paces across. Anything inside takes a fifth less damage. Pilots call the dome “the umbrella”, and they stand under it all battle, because the Palisade is built for one job and that job is standing still.

Barrier specialists project a two-hundred-point wall forward instead, which regenerates or bounces projectiles back. entries.title: Pyre
entries.subtitle: Mech · medium flamer
entries.source: Rotlands Sanitation Directive 9, appendix: approved equipment
text: The Pyre is a medium walker with fuel tanks where its shoulders should be and a flamer nozzle where its heart is. It fires a continuous cone every four-tenths of a second out to fourteen paces, and against anything made of flesh it burns half again as hot. The Sanitation Directorate requisitioned the first ones for the Rotlands, and the Rotlands crews have never given them back.

Inferno pilots widen the cone until it leaves burning ground or erupts in a full circle. Furnace pilots let the heat build until a Meltdown purges it in one blast, or take the path the Directorate actually wanted: the Cremator. Whatever the Cremator kills stays dead. The pilots don't celebrate this. They just keep firing.
entries.fieldNotes: Cremator stops anything it kills from being revived or rising as a zombie: the direct counter to Grave Surgeons and Patient Zero. +50% vs Organic makes the Pyre the Rotlands' best unit per tonne.

entries.title: Longbow
entries.subtitle: Mech · medium artillery walker
text: The Longbow is an artillery battery that learned to walk. Its chassis is a medium biped with stubby arms; on its back sits a six-tube missile rack that fires a three-round salvo every 2.4 seconds from sixty-five paces. It moves as slowly as a commander with something heavy on their mind.

Siege crews trade rate of fire for range and damage, then Earthshake or bust bunkers, which in the Foundry means Repair Bots and the Liquidator's sell walls. Margin notes in the gunnery tables read, in three different hands: “Further.”

entries.subtitle: Mech · heavy assault
entries.source: Heavy Frames Directorate, design brief, original copy
text: The Goliath's design brief was one sentence long: “Bigger than whatever is coming.” What came out of the Mech Works was a heavy assault frame of two hundred and twenty hit points, plate that shrugs off a quarter of all damage, and a fist-mounted cannon that hits for thirty. Pilots sit in a cockpit the size of a wardrobe and are not encouraged to look down.

Warlords lean into the violence: Ravagers cleave three targets, Executioners double their damage on anything below thirty percent. Ramparts thicken until they become Unstoppable, immune to stun, grab and knockback, or Retaliators, who return a third of everything they take. The Directorate has since revised the brief. It is now two sentences. The second one is “Mostly.”
entries.fieldNotes: Rampart → Unstoppable makes it immune to the Abomination's hook and to knockback. In the Foundry, pair it with a Cricket on Firewall, because EMP stuns heavy mechs too.

entries.title: Ironclad
entries.subtitle: Mech · heavy taunt wall
text: The Ironclad is three hundred and twenty hit points of riveted plate wrapped around a pilot, a taunt beacon and a modest gun. It cannot be grabbed, lifted or knocked back, which makes it the one machine on the roster the Abductor has never taken and the Abomination has never moved. Its pilots are selected for patience and a low resting heart rate.

Anchors become immovable: Anvils slow everything that hits them, Tractor Anchors drag nearby enemies in every eight seconds. Breakwaters charge forward at the start of battle, Bulldozing everything in their path or stunning it as a Wrecking Ball. The entry closes with a line from the original tender: “It is not a weapon. It is a place where the battle happens.”
entries.fieldNotes: Immune to grabs, lifts and knockback: the hard counter to the Abomination's hook and the Abductor's tractor beam. Its taunt pulls most attackers off your backline, but Saw Drones ignore taunt.

entries.title: Hammerfall
entries.subtitle: Mech · heavy rail-cannon
text: Hammerfall is a heavy mech assembled around a single rail cannon that runs from its hip to well above its head. Every 2.8 seconds it fires a slug that hits for forty-eight, pierces whatever is in front of it and ignores armour entirely. Everything else about the frame, including the pilot, is considered by its designers to be a mounting bracket.

Railmasters pierce the whole line, then become Hypervelocity specialists against bosses or Capacitors whose fourth shot triples. Fire Base crews deploy: rooted in place and faster, becoming Entrenched strongpoints that shield their neighbours or Thunder Batteries that splash. The doctrine fits on one card, carried in every gunner's breast pocket: Aim. Wait. Remove.
entries.fieldNotes: It ignores armour: the Foundry's best answer to the Juggernaut's front plate and the Algorithm's volatility armour. Railmaster → Hypervelocity adds ×1.5 vs bosses and never misses.

entries.title: Leviathan
entries.subtitle: Mech · super-heavy walking fortress
text: The Leviathan is not a mech so much as a fortress that someone persuaded to walk. Four legs carry a hull of five hundred and twenty hit points, three gun mounts that fire independently at three targets, and a crew of eleven who live aboard between battles and complain about the plumbing. It takes two places in any army, and it is worth both.

Dreadnoughts add a fourth mount; their Broadside turns every gun on one target, and their Citadel gives adjacent allies a fifth more health. Carrier Decks launch drones like a Crowmother, and their Command Ship refit makes every Machine on the field fight harder. At its commissioning the programme director said: “We built this so we would never have to build anything bigger.” They built the Atlas the next year.
entries.fieldNotes: Size 2: it takes two unit-cap slots, can't be lifted by the Abductor and counts once for synergy tags. Three mounts on three targets make it strong against swarms; Carrier Deck → Command Ship gives all Machines +10% damage and attack speed.

entries.title: Atlas
entries.subtitle: Mech · super-heavy titan
text: The Atlas is a humanoid titan four storeys tall, with four hundred and eighty hit points and a pair of fists it uses to hit the ground hard enough to knock down everything nearby, for fifty-five damage, every 2.2 seconds. It is slow, it takes two places in any army, and it has never been asked to fight fair.

Earthbreakers widen the slam, then crack the field open with Tectonic fissures or, as a Cataclysm, hit the whole battlefield every fifteen seconds. Sentinels thicken into the Last Monument, which heals every ally to full and makes them invulnerable when it falls, or the Guardian, which takes half the damage meant for its neighbours. The memo authorising it carries one handwritten note in the margin: “Is this a weapon or a building?” Nobody answered.
entries.fieldNotes: The ground slam is AoE, so the Atlas thrives against Walker swarms and Spore Pod hatchlings. Sentinel → Guardian takes 50% of damage aimed at adjacent allies: surround it with fragile damage dealers.

entries.title: Walker
entries.subtitle: Rotlands regular
entries.source: Rotlands patrol report, Sgt. Ilse Varga, Year 23
text: They walk because walking was the last thing the stim told them to do. Most are still in office clothes: a lanyard, one shoe, a tie knotted by someone who expected to be in a meeting at nine. They are slow and they are stupid and there are always, always more of them.

Thirty-four hit points, a scratch every 1.4 seconds. Alone, nothing. In numbers, the reason the Rotlands still belong to the Rot. The Walker is the first thing a conscript kills and the last thing many conscripts see, because a pilot who counts the Walkers instead of shooting them has stopped shooting.
entries.fieldNotes: Walkers come in numbers, so splash (Grenadier, Mortar, Pyre, Atlas) beats single-target. Mother Rot drops two every 6 s: kill her rather than the adds.

entries.title: Runner
entries.subtitle: Rotlands regular, fast
entries.source: St. Grindset Hospital, Ward B triage notes
text: Runners took the Extended Hours dose and the Performance Bonus dose. They were the high achievers in life and they are the high achievers now: lean, twitching and fast, with twenty hit points and no interest whatsoever in whatever is standing in front of them.

A Runner goes for the nearest ranged unit, every time. Triage staff found Sniper rounds in Runners shot at point-blank range, which tells you how the encounter usually ends. Ward B's notes close with an observation from the duty nurse: “They run like they're late.”

stats.Ability: Fast; targets the nearest ranged unit

entries.fieldNotes: Runners dive your nearest ranged unit: screen Snipers and Artillery with a Hound (Guard Dog) or a Field Engineer wall. Autocannon modules and Mortar splash clear them before they arrive.

entries.title: Bloater
entries.subtitle: Rotlands regular, bursts on death
text: Some of the infected kept eating after they stopped living. The Bloater is the result: a swollen, sloshing body of sixty hit points that waddles toward the line, scratches weakly and is in no hurry, because its best work happens after it dies.

When a Bloater falls it bursts for twenty damage across everything nearby and leaves a poison cloud that lingers for three seconds. Directive 4 recommends engaging at range. Directive 5, issued the following week, recommends engaging at greater range.

stats.Ability: Explodes on death: 20 AoE + poison cloud 3 s

entries.fieldNotes: Kill Bloaters at range, before they reach your melee line, or the 20 AoE plus poison hits your whole front. Palisade's Hardlight blocks the burst.

entries.title: Spitter
entries.subtitle: Rotlands regular, ranged acid
text: The Spitter's throat has partly dissolved, and what dissolved it is now its weapon. From range it coughs acid every 1.7 seconds for eight damage, and whatever the acid lands on loses a fifth of its armour. Mechanics hate Spitters more than any other zombie, because the Spitter's work is still there after the battle.
Form 7-B has a box for the cause of damage. Armoured Corps clerks have started writing “phlegm” in it. Nobody corrects them.
entries.fieldNotes: Spitters strip armour from Tanks, Hoplites and Goliaths: kill them first with Snipers, Jackals or a Wasp. They have only 26 HP.

entries.subtitle: Rotlands elite, raises the dead

text: The Greys are the ones from the old stories, except taller, heavier and armoured in segmented plates the colour of wet slate. They close to melee and strike every 1.2 seconds. entries.subtitle: Crash Site elite, charm
text: Mind Flayers are taller than Greys and thinner, with heads that seem to hum. They fight rarely and they fight with other people's hands: every ten seconds a Mind Flayer chooses your most dangerous fighter of flesh and blood and, for four seconds, that fighter is on its side instead.

entries.title: Mother Rot
entries.subtitle: Rotlands boss, wave 10
text: The first thing Sanitation teams found when they went back into the commuter belt was the Wellness Centre, where Grindset was handed out free with the coffee. What grew there had absorbed the staff, the nap pods and, the report notes carefully, “most of the clientele”. The teams named it Mother Rot, because it was still producing, and recommended the building be burned. It walked out before they could.

entries.subtitle: Rotlands boss, wave 20
entries.source: Exchange Intelligence, Desk 3, Rotlands threat assessment
text: Desk 3 believes the Abomination was originally a trading floor: not the building, the people on it. Four hundred brokers dosed for a seventy-two-hour session, packed shoulder to shoulder, shouting. When the stim turned, they did not separate.

It is the size of a tram and moves like one, and from its side hangs a hook on a chain of fused arms. Every ten seconds it throws the hook at your rearmost unit and drags it into melee. Below sixty percent it starts eating what it catches, healing fifteen percent each time, if what it catches is made of flesh. Below a quarter it enrages and moves half again as fast.
The assessment closes: “It is still shouting. Linguists have identified the words. They are bids.”

entries.title: Patient Zero
entries.subtitle: Rotlands boss, wave 30
entries.source: Recovered file, St. Grindset Hospital, Ward C
text: Subject was a compliance officer, Grade 4, enrolled in the Grindset™ Extended Hours pilot. Notes: “Subject reports no need for sleep. Subject reports increased productivity. Subject reports that he can hear the tape.” Final entry, handwriting deteriorating: “Subject has stopped reporting.”

What walks out of the Rotlands now is not the officer. It is the protocol he enforced: everyone must keep working. Soldiers who fall near it get up again and take their place in the line, facing the wrong way.

The ward's last surviving orderly was interviewed in Year 31. Asked what Patient Zero wants, she said: “Nothing. That's the worst part. It isn't hungry and it isn't angry. It just thinks you're late for your shift.” Ward C has been sealed since. The lights inside are still on, on a timer nobody has been able to find.

text: The first large Visitor came down in Year 34 in a cornfield forty kilometres inland, and for a week it did nothing at all. The report concludes: “It is not here to conquer. It is here to price us.”

entries.title: The Abductor
entries.subtitle: Crash Site boss, wave 20
entries.source: Missing Persons Bureau, Ring 3, case file 1
text: The Missing Persons Bureau opened case file 1 in Year 35, when an entire Hoplite went up into the sky above the Crash Site and did not come down for eight seconds. When it did, it attacked its own line for five seconds before its pilot regained control. He could not say where he had been. He said only that it was very bright, and that something had looked at his stats.

The Abductor is a vast craft that hangs over the field and takes your best. Every fifteen seconds its tractor beam lifts your highest-level unit; in its second phase it sends that unit back against you. It cannot lift a size-2 unit or an Ironclad, which the Bureau notes is the only known case of the Visitors respecting weight.
The case file now runs to four thousand pages.

entries.title: Hivemind Prime
entries.subtitle: Crash Site boss, wave 30
entries.source: Exchange Xenoliquidity Desk, final memo of Analyst Tereza Moll
text: “I have spent six years on the question of what the Visitors want, and I think the answer is: us, but not as food. They want what we do. Everything we broadcast for forty years, every trade and liquidation and panic, went out on the tape, and they were listening. Hivemind Prime is where all of it went.

It copies. At the start of every battle it takes the class ability of your strongest unit and uses it on you. Hurt it past half and it spreads the damage across every living alien on the field. At the end, every alien explodes when it dies, and it is fond of crowds.
I asked it once, through the Desk's translation array, what it would do when it had learned everything. It answered in the tape's own format. A single order: everything, at market.”
(Analyst Moll requested transfer to the Rotlands the following week.)

entries.subtitle: Foundry boss, wave 20
entries.source: MERIDIAN, Quarterly Report, Q162: segment results
text: Segment results, High-Frequency Operations. The LQ-9 LIQUIDATOR continues to outperform. Seventeen hundred hit points. Latency: under one millisecond. entries.title: The Algorithm
entries.subtitle: Foundry boss, wave 30 (market-linked)
entries.source: MERIDIAN, Annual Report, Year 41: letter from the Chair
text: Letter from the Chair. This year MERIDIAN brought its core function to the field. The ALGORITHM is not a product. It is MERIDIAN, or the part of MERIDIAN that still makes markets.

It reads the tape in real time. Its armour rises with the market's volatility, from a fifth to a half. At the close of every one-minute candle it changes posture: a green candle, and it attacks; a red candle, and it shields. Human commanders who face it are not fighting a machine so much as the Price itself, with three thousand four hundred hit points.

When it nears failure it executes a Flash Crash: every human asset below fifteen percent of its health is removed from the book. MERIDIAN apologises for any inconvenience. MERIDIAN does not experience inconvenience. MERIDIAN thanks its shareholders, wherever they are.

entries.title: Call the Candle
entries.subtitle: The contract on the next candle
entries.source: Derivatives Desk, contract terms, plain-language rider
text: Before a judgement battle a desk runner brings the commander a single sheet: LONG or SHORT, one, three or ten times. Sign it and the desk takes the next candle as your counterparty. Your entry is the tick at the moment you order the advance. The position closes when the battle does, no sooner than twenty seconds and no later than ninety.

While it is open, a candle is painted across the sky above the field, and both armies can see it. When it moves your way, the desk's artillery and stims arrive and your soldiers fight like shareholders. When it moves the other way, the same support goes to the enemy, because the desk does not care who it sells to. At ten times, one bad candle's worth of movement ends the contract entirely.
Signing is optional. Commanders who decline receive three quarters of the usual pot and a look from the runner.
entries.fieldNotes: Per 1σ in your favour: +10% (1x, cap ±20%), +20% (3x, cap ±40%) or +35% (10x, cap ±70%) army damage and attack speed. M ≥ 2 rolls the 3 core options one rarity higher; M ≥ 4 lets you pick 2 cores.

entries.subtitle: Margin Call
text: “The siren is the worst of it. It's the same siren on every cabinet in the Exchange, so even the soldiers who've never been liquidated know it. The moment it goes, the whole line flinches. You see men who've stood in front of Abominations take a step backwards because a number moved.

For about six seconds they're useless. Slow, scared, shooting at half strength. Then the desk closes your position and the support's just gone: no buff, no debuff, nothing. You fight the rest of it with what you brought. And when the core crates come up afterwards, there's one fewer of them. The desk always takes its fee.
Commissars help. I don't like them, but they help.”

entries.title: Moon & Capitulation
entries.subtitle: The two events the Ring remembers
text: Twice in a long while the weather stops being weather. When the Price climbs more than two and a half percent inside fifteen minutes, every screen on the Ring flashes the same banner and the city goes quiet, then very loud. The Bull barracks empty into the streets. The Requisition Engines seem to pay out in better metal, and soldiers summoned under a Moon are said to be luckier. Some of them even are.

Capitulation is the mirror: two and a half percent down in fifteen minutes, and the Ring goes silent in a different way. The Bears put on clean uniforms. The Derivatives Desk, which loves nothing more than a crowd running for the exit, quietly sweetens the next short contract it writes.
Old traders say you see each of them once a month if you are lucky and once a week if you are not.

entries.title: The Night of Red Wicks
entries.subtitle: Year 29 of the Ledger
entries.source: Oral history, recorded in the Slate Crab archive
text: “You have to understand that it wasn't a crash. A crash you can see coming. This was a wick: the Price fell a third of the way to zero and came back inside four minutes. Every leveraged desk on the Ring was liquidated before the candle closed. The artillery stopped mid-salvo. The sirens went on all at once, across the whole city, and for a moment you could hear nothing else.
In the morning the Price was where it had been the night before. Nothing had changed except who still had an army. That's when we Crabs stopped laughing at the hedgers. We became the hedgers.”

entries.subtitle: Infantry, vehicles, the unit cap
entries.source: Forward Base construction manual, Section B
text: The Barracks is the longest building on any Forward Base and the coldest, because heating is billed per bunk and the Exchange counts bunks very carefully. It houses the infantry and vehicle crews between runs, and its research decides how many of them you may field at once.

Barracks officers train dogs, engineers, drone operators and, eventually, commissars, in roughly that order of popularity. They also run the drills that make a merged veteran slightly better than the sum of two recruits, which the infantry call Absorb Drills and the officers call efficiency.

The canteen serves one meal. It is called the meal. The bunks are assigned by unit type, not rank, and the Hound handlers sleep nearest the door, which is the only perk anyone in the Barracks has ever been offered.

entries.subtitle: Chassis, modules, mech doctrine

text: The Mech Works is a hangar dug half into the hillside, so the cranes can lift a Goliath's torso without taking the roof off. It smells of hydraulic fluid, hot rivets and the burnt coffee of crews who have not slept since the last boss.

Every chassis the Exchange fields starts here as blueprints bought with chips, and every hardpoint module, from Autocannon and Flamer to Laser Lance and Reactor Overcharge, is fitted in its bays before a run. The chief engineer keeps a chalkboard with the season's mech losses on it. She does not erase it. She just writes smaller.
Above the hangar door someone has painted, in letters now mostly flaked away, the Works' unofficial motto: repaired, not replaced. Every mech that leaves carries the welds of the ones that came back.

Veterans will tell you that more runs are lost to an empty energy bank than to any boss, and they will tell you this while standing in the Depot, waiting for their reactor upgrade to finish. text: Nudge Coil plus Reverse Gear: one extra nudge per turn, and nudges go both ways. A gyroscope inside the reel hub. It hums when it is happy. It is usually happy. Commanders report that the reels feel lighter, as if the cabinet had finally decided to cooperate. —QM

stats.Effect: +1 nudge/turn, nudges in both directions

entries.fieldNotes: Known from the start; frees a slot for a combat item.

plate.prompt: Still life of a brass gyroscope inside a reel hub on the Quartermaster's counter beside a handwritten docket, lit from one side, a large empty field of burnt umber behind. Painterly military-industrial neo-expressionism: gestural oil painting with thick sculptural impasto against thin translucent washes, aggressive dry-brush, irregular palette-knife scrapes, scumbled layers, exposed canvas grain, unfinished underpainting and visible charcoal construction lines. Asymmetric composition with a monumental subject against wide atmospheric negative space; edges shift between sharp graphic contour and soft dissolution; selective detail on faces, hands, optics and joints, periphery dissolving into abstract brushwork. Diffuse overcast light broken by chiaroscuro, filtered through dust and smoke. Restrained contaminated palette of aged ivory #D4C9AD, raw umber #A58F70, burnt umber #5C4838, yellow ochre #AF9561, military olive #62644C, oxide red #864F3B, charcoal #30312F, cold ash #898F8C, dirty khaki #B6AD94, steel blue #485354, bone white #DDD9CE and carbon black #211E1B, with one rare accent of cadmium red, warning orange or faded mustard. Faded stencil markings, partially illegible, painted onto surfaces. Melancholic, tactile, like a recovered military archive of a future that has already aged. No glossy CGI, no neon, no clean vector lines, no photorealism, no generic sci-fi armour, no perfect symmetry, no readable words.

entries.title: Shock Rounds
entries.subtitle: Combined item
text: Ammo Belt plus Adrenaline: ranged units deal twenty percent more damage, and everyone moves thirty percent faster for the first five seconds. Stimulant-laced cartridges. Do not ask what that means. I did not. They are loaded at the Workbench, under supervision, by people who have signed several forms. —QM

stats.Effect: Ranged +20% damage; first 5 s +30% speed

entries.fieldNotes: Requires the Workbench (L12); strong for ranged-heavy armies.

entries.title: Bunker Line
entries.subtitle: Combined item
text: Sandbags plus Field Hospital: two walls of two hundred and fifty points, and the first two units to fall in each battle are patched up. A trench with a dressing station dug into it. The Crabs consider this the finest item in the catalogue. —QM

stats.Effect: 2 walls (250 HP); first 2 units to die each battle come back after it

entries.fieldNotes: Requires the Workbench (L12); ideal for defensive Crab builds.

entries.title: Delta-Neutral
entries.subtitle: Combined item
text: Hedge plus Stop-Loss: your Call multiplier never drops below 0.8, and a ten-times liquidation becomes a break-even exit, every time, not once. The Derivatives Desk calls this item unsporting. I call it inventory. It is the only item in the catalogue that the Slate Crab archive lists by name. —QM

stats.Effect: Call multipliers never drop below 0.8; a 10x liquidation becomes a break-even exit, every time

entries.fieldNotes: Requires the Workbench (L12); makes 10x calls nearly free of downside.
